cards.front: Before writing any production code, what should you write first, and why does it need to come before implementation?
cards.back: A short design document (usually one markdown page) stating the success criteria, failure handling, cost/latency budget, and trust boundary. It comes first because every production layer (eval, error handling, cost tuning, security) is built from it - writing it first defines what 'correct' means instead of letting you rationalize whatever the model produces later.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.cloze_text: A production design document holds four decisions: {{c1::success criteria}} (what the feature must produce, stated specifically enough to grade), {{c2::failure handling}} (which failures the system must survive and what happens for each), {{c3::cost and latency budget}} (the ceiling the system must stay under and the reliability floor it can't trade away), and {{c4::trust boundary}} (which inputs are untrusted and what actions the system may take).
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: What does an eval actually do, and what does it NOT do, according to the 'thermometer' analogy in this lesson?
cards.back: An eval works like a thermometer: it doesn't make the patient (feature) healthier, it just gives you a number you can trust. It's a set of input cases, expected behaviors, and grades - before you have one, 'done' is a feeling; after, it's a score on a fixed set of cases.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: Why should you write the eval before building the feature, rather than after?
cards.back: Writing it first forces you to define success before implementation begins. If you write it after, you risk rationalizing whatever output the model happens to produce instead of holding it to a predefined standard.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.cloze_text: The three eval grading methods, matched to output shape: {{c1::exact or string match}} for a single correct form (cheapest, but fails any valid paraphrase); {{c2::code-graded check}} for structured output like valid JSON or a value in range (checks format, not quality); and {{c3::LLM-as-judge}} for open-ended quality like faithfulness or instruction-following (most expensive and noisiest, but the only one that scales to judgment calls).
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: A feature must return three capital cities as a JSON array. One run returns the correct three cities but in a different order than the reference string. How does an exact-match grader score this versus a code grader that parses the JSON and checks membership, and why the difference?
cards.back: Exact match scores it zero - the characters don't line up even though the answer is correct. The code grader scores it well, because all three cities are present and the structure is valid. Exact match checks characters; a code check validates the underlying rule (membership), not surface form.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: When building an LLM-as-judge grading prompt, why should you ask it to return strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning alongside the score, instead of just the score alone?
cards.back: Without that, models drift toward a safe middle number (usually around six) regardless of actual quality. Asking the judge to produce reasoning first is what anchors the score to something specific instead of a vague, non-committal estimate.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: How do you calibrate an LLM-as-judge so its scores are actually defensible, and why does skipping this step (as most people do) matter?
cards.back: Run the judge on a set of cases a human has already labeled, and measure how often the judge agrees with the human. Skipping this is exactly what makes an uncalibrated judge untrustworthy - a judge that disagrees with human labels half the time produces a number that looks rigorous but has no value. If agreement is low, tighten the rubric (clarify what each score means, add a good/bad example) and re-measure.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: According to this lesson, is a larger eval set with noisier automated grading, or a small set of hand-graded cases, more likely to reveal a regression - and why?
cards.back: A larger set with noisier automated grading usually reveals more. Twenty cases including irregular or edge inputs will catch a break that three carefully chosen cases never exercise - the point of an eval is coverage, not a perfect rubric.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: When iterating on a failing eval score, why should you change only one component (prompt, tools, or model) at a time rather than several at once?
cards.back: If you rewrite the prompt, add examples, and switch the model all in one pass and the score moves, you've learned nothing about which change caused it. Changing one lever at a time is slower per iteration but teaches you what actually drives the score, which pays off over the life of the feature.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: Why can a steady average eval score be misleading, even when a prompt change had a real effect on individual cases?
cards.back: A steady average can hide a change that fixed three cases and broke three others - the gains and losses cancel out in the aggregate. The per-case breakdown shows this immediately, while the average conceals it.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Defining done before you ship: evals and a calibrated judge

cards.front: A feature extracting a date field passed all its validation checks (non-empty message, populated date field, well-formed date) yet still extracted the wrong value from a message mentioning two dates. What does this reveal about the limits of input and output validation?
cards.back: Validation confirms a value is the right shape (well-formed, populated) - it cannot confirm the value is the right one (semantically correct). Both dates in the message were well-formed, so every check passed even though the wrong one was extracted.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · The demo that passed and the edge case that did not

cards.front: A team's date-extraction feature passed a dozen manual demo checks before shipping, then extracted the wrong date from a two-date message in production. What was the actual root cause the postmortem identified, and what was explicitly NOT the cause?
cards.back: The root cause was a missing graded (holdout) set: nobody had defined expected behavior for a two-date message as a checkable case, because the dozen manual checks all used single-date messages, the input the builder happened to picture. The review found no bug in the model or in the prompt itself.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · The demo that passed and the edge case that did not

cards.front: In the two-date extraction postmortem, what specifically did adding the failing case to the eval set accomplish, and what did it NOT do?
cards.back: The eval did not fix the extraction (a prompt change, most likely naming which date to extract, did that). The eval detected the failure, documented the expected behavior as a checkable case, and guarded against the same regression on every future change.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · The demo that passed and the edge case that did not

cards.front: What technique does this lesson suggest for finding edge-case inputs, like a message containing two dates, before a customer surfaces them in production?
cards.back: Ask the model to enumerate edge cases that could break the current implementation (for example, two dates in one sentence, no date at all, a relative date like 'next Tuesday'), then turn the plausible ones into graded cases with a human-checked expected output.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · The demo that passed and the edge case that did not

cards.front: When authoring an eval dataset, why is an expected_behavior field that's empty, or filled with something vague like 'a good summary,' a problem, and what should it contain instead?
cards.back: An eval's expected_behavior must name a concrete, checkable output specific to that exact input case - for example, for a meeting transcript with three assigned action items, 'a summary that lists all three action items with their owners,' not a restatement of the input or a vague quality wish. A vague or empty expected_behavior gives the grader nothing specific to check against.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Complete a partial eval for a summarization feature

cards.front: A judge prompt defines score bands (1 to 3, 4 to 7, 8 to 10) but leaves what each band means undefined. Why does this matter, and how should each band be anchored?
cards.back: An unanchored scale produces a number that isn't comparable across runs or defensible in review. Each band should be anchored to a concrete description: 1 to 3 means it misses required content entirely, 4 to 7 means partial (some required content present, some missing), 8 to 10 means complete and faithful to the expected behavior.
cards.extra: M4 · Evals & Judges · Complete a partial eval for a summarization feature

cards.cloze_text: The four test levels, from narrowest to broadest scope: {{c1::unit test}} (isolates one function on its own), {{c2::functional test}} (checks one Claude call returns the expected shape), {{c3::integration test}} (exercises the handoff between two components), and {{c4::end-to-end test}} (runs the whole flow the way a user would).
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: Why do most silent production failures live specifically at the integration test level, rather than being caught by unit or functional tests?
cards.back: Because each side of a handoff (for example, a retrieval result passed into a model call) can pass its own test in isolation while the handoff between them is broken. A unit test only checks one function on its own; a functional test only checks one call's shape - neither exercises the seam where two components connect.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: A test tells you a failure exists. What does a trace add on top of that, and why does it matter?
cards.back: A trace records each step of a run (the prompt, tool calls, intermediate outputs, and timing), letting you see exactly which step produced the bad result. Without a trace, a failed eval tells you something is wrong but not where - this is the difference between a five-minute fix and a day spent tracing the workflow by hand.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: What's the reasoning for using a cheap classification step to route queries between a fetch-once retrieval path and an iterative agentic-search path, rather than picking one strategy for all traffic?
cards.back: Defaulting everything to iterative search inflates cost and latency on simple questions a single fetch would answer; defaulting everything to a static fetch-once index gives shallow answers on questions that need several passes. A cheap router call reads the query and picks the right path, so you pay for iteration only when the query needs it.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: According to this lesson, when should you skip building a query router for retrieval strategy entirely?
cards.back: When every query in your traffic is the same shape - the router only earns its cost when traffic is mixed between simple lookups and multi-step questions.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: What is the specific weakness of an end-to-end test, even though it catches breaks that only appear when the whole flow runs together?
cards.back: It is the slowest test to run and the hardest to localize - it sees only the final result, not which internal step caused the failure.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Testing and tracing

cards.front: In a RAG pipeline, retrieve() passed its unit test and the model-call function passed its functional test, yet the end-to-end test failed because the model answered from memory instead of using retrieved context. What was the actual defect?
cards.back: The format contract between the two components was never defined: retrieve() returned a list of chunk dictionaries, while build_prompt() expected a plain string. The context arrived malformed, so the model ignored it and answered from its own memory.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · The pieces passed and the seam broke

cards.front: Why couldn't a unit test or a functional test have caught the retrieve()/build_prompt() format mismatch described in this lesson?
cards.back: A unit test couldn't catch it because each unit (retrieve, the model call) worked correctly on its own. A functional test couldn't catch it because the model call worked fine on well-formed input. Only a test that drives the two components together with real retrieved data exercises the seam where the mismatch lives.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · The pieces passed and the seam broke

cards.front: In a trace, a unit test and a functional test both pass but the end-to-end test fails at the point where one component's output is passed into another. What does this pattern tell you about where the bug must live, and what's the right first move?
cards.back: Since both components already pass in isolation, the bug cannot be inside either one - it must be in the handoff between them (for example, one side returns a shape the other side doesn't correctly read). The right move is to align the handoff itself and add an integration test on that exact seam, not to edit either component that's already passing its own test.
cards.extra: M4 · Testing & Tracing · Diagnose which test level a failure belongs to

cards.front: What single question determines whether a production failure should be classified as retriable versus terminal?
cards.back: Would waiting and trying the exact same request again plausibly work? If yes, it's retriable (for example, a rate limit clears with time). If not, it's terminal (for example, a malformed request will fail identically no matter how many times you retry it).
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.cloze_text: On the Anthropic API, {{c1::429}} (rate limit) and {{c2::529}} (temporary overload) are retriable, as are 5xx server errors like {{c3::500}} (internal error) and {{c4::504}} (timeout). {{c5::400}} (bad request) and {{c6::401}} (auth failure) are terminal.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: Why is the safe default to treat an ambiguous error as terminal rather than retriable, when you're unsure how to classify it?
cards.back: A failure incorrectly classified as terminal fails loudly and gets fixed. A failure incorrectly classified as retriable hammers the service with retries and hides the real problem behind a wall of failures - the asymmetry favors defaulting to terminal.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: The Anthropic client libraries already auto-retry transient failures with progressive delays. What mistake does this lesson warn against making on top of that built-in behavior?
cards.back: Adding your own retry loop on top of the SDK's without coordinating them - two retry loops wrapped around the same call multiply attempts against a rate limit instead of capping them. Decide where retries live: either let the SDK handle transient cases and reserve your own code for application-specific fallbacks, or turn the SDK's retries down and own the full path yourself.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: When a 429 or 529 response includes a retry-after header, how should your retry logic use it relative to exponential backoff?
cards.back: Treat retry-after as the authoritative wait time when it's present - the service is telling you exactly when capacity returns, which is more precise than guessing. Fall back to exponential backoff only when the header is absent.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: When your code runs a tool and it fails, why must the result be returned to Claude with is_error explicitly set to true, rather than returning an empty result?
cards.back: With is_error set, the model knows the tool failed and can react: try a different approach, ask for clarification, or stop. Without it, the model treats the empty result as valid data and continues reasoning on top of it, producing a confident but wrong answer built on missing data.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: A model refusal comes back as a 200 status with stop_reason of refusal. Why won't a standard retriable-versus-terminal status-code classifier catch this, and how should it be handled?
cards.back: A refusal is a 200 at the HTTP layer, so a classifier that only inspects status codes won't flag it. It should be treated as fail-fast: raise it rather than retry, since the model made a content decision, not a transient error - retrying it or silently treating it as valid output are both wrong.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: Timeouts are generally treated as retriable, but this lesson notes an exception. What does repeated timeouts on the same expensive request actually signal, versus a single timeout?
cards.back: A single timeout is usually retriable, since the work may simply have taken longer than the client waited. But repeated timeouts on an expensive request is a signal to fix the request itself (for example, reduce its scope), not to keep retrying it.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Surviving production failure: tool errors

cards.front: A developer never added error handling to an API-calling loop because it always returned successfully during development. Why did development never surface the problem that production immediately did?
cards.back: Development traffic is low-volume and rarely hits conditions like rate limits, timeouts, or transient network drops - so the code path that would handle them was never exercised, and therefore never written, until real production traffic hit a limit.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · The call that never failed in development

cards.front: After a rate-limit error crashed a request in production, a developer's first instinct was to add immediate retries in a tight loop. Why did this make the problem worse instead of fixing it?
cards.back: Each instant retry counts as another request against the same rate limit, deepening it rather than waiting for it to clear. The real fix was exponential backoff with a capped number of attempts, honoring the retry-after value when present, not hammering the endpoint faster.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · The call that never failed in development

cards.front: A retry function catches every exception, sleeps with time.sleep(0) between attempts, and retries up to 5 times before raising. What's wrong with this implementation, and what three fixes does it need?
cards.back: Defect: there's no real backoff (sleep(0) retries instantly), and it retries every exception including terminal statuses like 400 that retrying can never fix - against a rate limit, each instant retry counts as another request and deepens the limit. Fixes: (1) honor the retry-after header first, falling back to exponential backoff with a cap; (2) grow the wait interval between attempts; (3) fail fast on terminal statuses (400, 401, 403, 404) instead of retrying them.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Repair the broken error and retry path

cards.cloze_text: Claude's capability tiers trade cost, latency, and capability against each other: {{c1::Fable}} is the most capable, for the most demanding reasoning, coding, and agentic work; {{c2::Opus}} handles demanding work above the Sonnet envelope; {{c3::Sonnet}} is the balanced default for most production workloads; {{c4::Haiku}} is built for speed and cost efficiency on tasks that fit its envelope.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: What does this lesson call the most common and most expensive model-selection mistake in production?
cards.back: Reaching for the most capable model by default, instead of making the cost and quality trade-off measurable. The discipline is to start with Sonnet, move up to Opus only when an eval shows Sonnet missing the quality bar, and move down to Haiku only when an eval shows the quality drop is acceptable for the task.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: Why might downgrading to a cheaper model tier actually be a bad trade even if it saves a few dollars a day?
cards.back: The cost of a mistake belongs in the calculation - if the quality drop from a lower-tier model introduces errors that carry significant downstream cost, the small per-day savings isn't a sound trade against that larger risk.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: Under what circumstance can a higher-tier, more capable model actually process a request faster and cheaper than a lower-tier one, despite its higher per-token cost?
cards.back: If the higher-tier model reaches a correct conclusion in fewer tokens than the lower-tier model would need, its total cost and latency for that request can come out lower despite the higher per-token rate.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: What is the default-model-plus-override routing pattern for model selection, and when should you skip it?
cards.back: Route the bulk of traffic to a balanced default model, and send specific request types to a larger or smaller model based on a cheap signal read from the request, such as task type, input length, or a difficulty classification, paying for the more capable model only where it's needed. Skip the router and pin one model when every request is the same shape.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: What's the decision rule for stepping up a model tier versus stepping down one, and what instrument gates both directions?
cards.back: Step up when an eval shows the current model failing on your traffic's hardest cases and the cost of a wrong answer is high. Step down when an eval shows a cheaper model holding the quality bar on the bulk of traffic. In both directions, the eval is the instrument - a model change is promoted on a measured score, not a guess.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Model selection in production

cards.front: A high-volume step classifies millions of short messages per day, and an eval shows Haiku holding the quality bar. Which model tier is the right call, and what's the deciding constraint?
cards.back: Haiku. The deciding constraint is cost-at-volume: since the eval confirms the quality bar still holds at that tier, paying for a larger, more expensive model buys nothing extra.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Choose the model and name the deciding constraint

cards.front: A multi-step agent plans a dependent refactor where a wrong early step is expensive, and an eval shows Sonnet missing the quality bar on the hardest cases. Which model tier is the right call, and why?
cards.back: Opus. The deciding constraint is quality on hard reasoning where the cost of a wrong answer is high - the eval shows Sonnet isn't sufficient, and an early mistake in a dependent chain is costly enough to justify the step up.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Choose the model and name the deciding constraint

cards.front: Traffic is mixed: most requests are simple lookups, a few are complex synthesis tasks. Why is picking one single model tier for all of it the wrong approach, and what should you do instead?
cards.back: A single model either overpays running a capable model on simple requests, or underperforms running a cheap model on complex ones. The right approach is to route: a Sonnet (or Haiku) default with an Opus override on the complex requests, because the deciding constraint is that the traffic itself is mixed.
cards.extra: M4 · Failure Handling & Model Selection · Choose the model and name the deciding constraint

cards.cloze_text: Observability for a Claude system means instrumenting three metrics per call: {{c1::token usage}} (input and output tokens), {{c2::latency}}, and {{c3::error rate}}.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: Why does per-call cost and latency logging matter more than just watching the total monthly bill?
cards.back: A cost spike without per-call logging only lets you ask why the bill is high. Per-call logging lets you ask which step, on which request type, is responsible, and get the answer directly from the data. A flow that looks uniformly expensive often has one step doing ninety percent of the spend, which is where optimization should focus.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: How does streaming a response change a user's perception of latency, even when the total generation time is unchanged?
cards.back: Streaming returns the first token as soon as it's ready instead of waiting for the full response. A response that starts arriving in 300ms feels faster than one delivered as a single block after two seconds, even if the total time to generate the full response is identical.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: Why can't you act on a tool_use block as soon as it appears in a streaming response, and what must you do instead?
cards.back: In a streaming call, tool_use blocks accumulate across multiple delta events (content_block_delta with input_json_delta) before they're complete - acting on a partial block produces malformed tool inputs. You must accumulate the deltas by index until the stream closes, then reconstruct the completed tool calls.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: What specifically does prompt caching store and let a later request skip, and why does that produce a saving?
cards.back: It stores the token-processing work done on a stretch of content (breaking the prompt into tokens and building the internal representations the model needs) so a later request with the same content up to a marked point reads that work back instead of recomputing it from scratch.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: How are prompt cache writes priced relative to reads, and what does that pricing imply about when caching is worth using?
cards.back: Cache writes cost a premium over base input tokens (1.25x for the 5-minute TTL, 2x for the 1-hour TTL), while cache reads cost a fraction of standard input (0.1x). The economics only work when reads outnumber writes - the same stable prefix must be hit by many requests to pay off.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.cloze_text: Prompt caching only helps a workload when three properties hold: the cached content must be {{c1::identical}} (the cache matches on an exact prefix, so any change before the breakpoint invalidates it), the same content must {{c2::recur soon}} (within the cache's lifetime, default five minutes, refreshed on each hit), and the cached prefix must be {{c3::long enough to clear the minimum length threshold}} (which varies by model).
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: What's the tradeoff you accept when you cache a prompt prefix, and what kind of content is therefore a poor caching candidate?
cards.back: Caching assumes the cached content is still correct on the later request - if the prefix needs to reflect data that can change, the cache may serve a stale version for as long as it lives. Content that must reflect live state is a poor caching candidate; a fixed system prompt or stable tool schema is safe because there's nothing in it to go stale.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: What does the Message Batches API trade away in exchange for its lower per-request cost, and what kind of work is it the wrong tool for?
cards.back: It trades latency for cost: you submit a batch and results come back within an asynchronous completion window rather than immediately, in exchange for costing less per request than the same calls made synchronously. It's the wrong tool for anything a user is waiting on, and the right tool for anything driven by a schedule, such as an overnight run, a backfill, or a scheduled report.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: Why do batching and prompt caching compound well together on a non-urgent job?
cards.back: The batch discount lowers the cost of each request, and caching lowers the cost of the repeated prefix inside each one - so a scheduled job that reuses the same context across many requests, such as a long fixed system prompt, benefits from both levers at once.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: Anthropic's own research system reported roughly what token cost multiplier for an orchestrator-worker (lead plus parallel subagents) setup versus a single-agent baseline, and on what kind of task does that multiplier actually pay off?
cards.back: Roughly 15x the tokens of a normal chat interaction, because every subagent spends its own tokens against its own context. It pays off on tasks that genuinely decompose into independent parts explorable in parallel, such as research across separate sources, not on tightly coupled tasks like coding, where each step depends on the last.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: Why does this lesson insist you set the reliability floor (retry budget, latency ceiling) before optimizing cost, rather than optimizing cost first and checking reliability after?
cards.back: Cost and reliability create opposing pressures, and cost is usually louder - a high bill shows up on a dashboard daily, while reliability problems look like occasional dismissible noise until they accumulate into an incident. If you optimize cost first, the louder pressure wins and you only discover you crossed the reliability floor after the fact. Setting the floor first makes reliability the fixed constraint and cost the thing optimized underneath it.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: What model-selection detail can reduce an orchestrator-worker pattern's cost multiplier while preserving coordination quality?
cards.back: Use a more capable model as the lead agent for planning and synthesis, and cheaper models for the subagents, so you're not paying top-tier rates across every parallel context.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Keeping cost, latency, and reliability in budget across agents

cards.front: After moving an over-orchestrated task (parallel subagents applied to tightly-coupled work) back to a single agent with the same context, what happened to cost and answer quality?
cards.back: The bill fell back down to what the single-agent work actually needed, and answer quality held steady - confirming the parallel fan-out had been adding cost without adding value on that particular task.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · The parallel fan-out that tripled the bill

cards.front: For a single-fact lookup against a stable reference corpus, what's the right configuration and cost lever, and why not add parallel agents or the Batches API here?
cards.back: A single small model with fetch-once retrieval; the lever is model choice, using the smallest model that works. There's no need to pay for iteration (agentic search) or fan-out (orchestrator-worker) on a lookup this simple.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Match each task to its agent type and cost lever

cards.front: For a broad research question that splits into independent parts explorable at once, what's the right configuration, and why does the orchestrator-worker token multiplier pay off here specifically?
cards.back: An orchestrator-worker setup with a large lead and small workers running in parallel; the lever is the parallel split. This is the one task shape that genuinely parallelizes, so the roughly 15x token multiplier buys real parallel exploration instead of being wasted.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Match each task to its agent type and cost lever

cards.front: For a user-facing request where the reply should feel instant, what's the right lever, and why does it help even if total generation time doesn't change?
cards.back: Streaming. It makes the response feel fast because the first token arrives almost immediately, even though the total time to generate the full response is the same as a non-streamed call.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Match each task to its agent type and cost lever

cards.front: For a cost-sensitive, non-urgent batch job that reuses the same context across many requests, what two levers should you combine, and why do they compound?
cards.back: The Message Batches API (roughly 50% cost reduction, trading latency for cost since no user is waiting) plus prompt caching (since the same context recurs across requests). They compound: batching lowers the cost of each request, and caching lowers the cost of the repeated prefix inside each one.
cards.extra: M4 · Cost & Orchestration · Match each task to its agent type and cost lever

cards.front: Why can't a model structurally tell the difference between the instructions you wrote and a hostile instruction embedded in a page it fetched?
cards.back: The model processes its entire context as one stream of tokens - there's no built-in boundary that separates trusted from untrusted data. Your system prompt, the user's message, and fetched content are all just text in the same sequence, so a forged instruction embedded in fetched content looks like just another command.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: Why doesn't trusting your own internal users solve the prompt injection problem?
cards.back: The hostile instruction typically arrives through content the agent retrieves, such as a fetched page, document, or tool result, not through the user's own prompt - so how much you trust the user is irrelevant to whether an injected instruction reaches the model.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: This lesson argues delimiters and careful prompt wording around untrusted content are only a soft boundary. Where does it say the reliable boundary actually lives instead?
cards.back: Not in the text itself - untrusted content can contain text that mimics your delimiters or argues persuasively for being an exception. The reliable boundary is in what the agent is allowed to do because of that text, meaning enforced action and access constraints, not prompt wording.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: How do a jailbreak and a prompt injection differ in what they target, and why does the layered defense look the same for both anyway?
cards.back: A jailbreak tries to get the model to ignore its own safety constraints; a prompt injection tries to hijack your application's instructions. Different targets, but the same defense shape applies to both: validate and constrain what reaches the model, and limit what the model is allowed to do as a result - defending only the prompt and not the action leaves the model free to cause damage once steered.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: Why does this lesson call least privilege a design principle rather than a configuration setting, in terms of what makes it different from model-level defenses like training and classifiers?
cards.back: It's the control that holds even when every other defense fails. If an injection gets past training and classifiers and the agent acts on a hostile instruction, the outcome is bounded entirely by what that agent's identity is allowed to do - a narrowly-scoped identity turns a successful injection into a denied action and a log entry instead of an incident.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: Beyond protecting secrets themselves, what other configuration does this lesson say deserves the same level of protection, and why?
cards.back: The agent's own auth or role configuration - anything that can modify it can effectively act with that identity. Whatever can widen the agent's permissions can also remove the control that limits the blast radius, so editing the agent's role is a privileged action that belongs behind the same protection as secrets.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: Why is a secret committed to configuration a permanent exposure even after you remove it from the current files?
cards.back: It lives on in repository history, so anyone who ever had read access to the repository may have accessed the secret. The correct response to a leaked secret is to rotate it - pulling secrets from environment variables or a managed secret store instead keeps them rotatable without changing the application itself.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: What's the distinction this lesson draws between a security rule that lives only in a prompt versus one enforced by a PreToolUse hook?
cards.back: A rule that lives only in a prompt is not enforced - the model can be talked out of following it. A hook that runs before a tool executes is an enforced control: it can actually block the tool call regardless of what the model decided to do.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: When multiple hooks or permission rules could apply to the same action and they disagree, what precedence order governs the outcome?
cards.back: Deny over ask over allow. A single deny rule blocks the action regardless of how many allow rules also apply - this ordering is what makes a hook a real boundary rather than a best-effort check.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.cloze_text: A financial or healthcare customer's security review typically asks three questions early: where is {{c1::data processed}} (data residency), how is {{c2::access logged}} (audit logging), and can an administrator {{c3::control the configuration centrally}} (managed configuration).
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: What does this lesson say about Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility across Claude models, and what should you do before committing to a ZDR-dependent deployment?
cards.back: ZDR eligibility varies by model and by platform and is not guaranteed for every model even under an existing ZDR agreement - not all current models are ZDR-eligible, and newer or higher-capability models may not yet have confirmed ZDR status. Confirm each model's current ZDR eligibility against the Anthropic Trust Center, and each cloud platform's own data-retention terms, at scoping time, since it may constrain model or platform selection.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: Hooks and least-privilege roles share a dependency that limits them. What is it, and how does OS-level sandboxing address that gap?
cards.back: Hooks and roles must explicitly cover the path or endpoint they're protecting - for example, a hook checking write_file doesn't automatically block a network call to an unreviewed endpoint. OS-level sandboxing isolates the agent at the process level instead of the rule level (filesystem isolation to the working directory, network isolation to named endpoints), so it holds even when a hook is missing, misconfigured, or bypassed.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Securing the integration against untrusted input and a regulated review

cards.front: A team reasoned that since their users are all internal and trusted, they didn't need to validate the pages their agent fetches. Why did an unexpected file write happen anyway?
cards.back: The instruction that caused the write didn't come from the trusted user - it came from a line embedded near the bottom of the fetched page, telling the agent to write its summary to a different path and ignore its prior instructions. Trusting the user does nothing to stop an injection that arrives through fetched content, since the user never asked for that write.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · The fetched page that gave the orders

cards.front: After discovering the agent had followed an injected instruction from a fetched page, what two-sided fix closed the gap?
cards.back: Treat fetched content as data to be examined, not as instructions to follow, and put a hook in front of the write tool that refuses an action triggered by untrusted input. This enforces the boundary before the tool runs rather than relying on the prompt alone - with the hook in place, the same injected line hits a denied write and an audit entry instead of succeeding.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · The fetched page that gave the orders

cards.front: Given a threat model of untrusted fetched content, a privileged write path, and a scoped identity under regulated review, a checkpoint asks you to assemble the minimal secure configuration from a PreToolUse hook, an explicit deny rule, an environment-variable secret reference, and an audit log. What's the trap in this question, and what's the right answer?
cards.back: The trap is assuming minimal means leaving something out. It actually means nothing beyond what the threat model requires, and this threat model requires all four: the hook blocks before the tool runs, the deny rule bounds the blast radius if the agent is steered, the environment-variable reference keeps the credential rotatable and out of source control, and the audit log gives a regulated reviewer the evidence trail they need.
cards.extra: M4 · Security · Assemble the minimal secure configuration for a fetch-and-write agent

cards.front: A single small function had three separate defects: one in the eval/test layer, one in error handling, one in the security boundary, and all three were real at once. What does this demonstrate about how you should diagnose a production system under review, versus assuming there's one root cause?
cards.back: Production defects can exist independently across layers at the same time - finding and fixing one, say the missing eval, says nothing about whether the others, the no-backoff retry loop or the unscoped write path, are also present. Each layer needs to be checked on its own terms rather than assuming a single bug explains everything.
cards.extra: M4 · Cumulative Task · Cumulative production-hardening task: find the three defects and explain each

cards.front: In the corrected version of the three-defect application, the eval, the retry and backoff fix, and the security hook are each applied independently. Why does it matter that these three fixes don't depend on or interfere with one another?
cards.back: Each fix sits at the layer it defends and reinforces the others rather than overlapping with them - the fixed write path and hook close the security boundary regardless of the retry logic, call_with_retry adds backoff regardless of the write path, and the graded holdout set checks correctness regardless of either. Because the fixes are orthogonal, each can be verified and shipped on its own layer's terms.
cards.extra: M4 · Cumulative Task · Cumulative production-hardening task: write the corrected version

cards.front: What is agentic search, and what does it cost you relative to a fixed one-time fetch?
cards.back: Letting the model issue its own queries, read the results, and refine across several rounds instead of fetching a fixed set of context once. It handles multi-step questions and changing corpora, at higher token and latency cost than a single fetch, but it avoids the staleness and infrastructure of a maintained index.
cards.extra: M4 · Key Takeaways · Key terms from this module

cards.cloze_text: {{c1::Exponential backoff}} is a retry strategy that waits a growing interval between attempts, up to a cap and a fixed number of tries, often with random jitter - it prevents immediate retries from deepening a rate limit, and honors a retry-after value when the response provides one.
cards.extra: M4 · Key Takeaways · Key terms from this module

cards.front: What makes a hook-based guardrail different from a rule stated in a system prompt, in terms of what a regulated review cares about?
cards.back: A hook-based guardrail is a check that runs at a fixed point in the Claude Code agent lifecycle, such as PreToolUse before a tool call, and can block an action and log it. Unlike a prompt instruction, it's an enforced control that runs before the protected action - that enforcement, not just the rule's wording, is what a regulated review cares about.
cards.extra: M4 · Key Takeaways · Key terms from this module

cards.front: What is the LLM-as-judge grading method, and under what condition does this lesson say it becomes trustworthy?
cards.back: A grading method that uses a second model call with a rubric to score open-ended outputs that no code rule can check, returning a score with reasoning. It's only trustworthy after you calibrate it against human-labeled cases and measure agreement - an uncalibrated judge just produces a confident-looking number.
